steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on optimal transport distances for directed, weighted graphs, with cell-cell communication networks as the case study. Cover existing graph distances, OT-based distances and why directed graphs are hard, our approach and evaluation, the contributions, and an outline of the paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Exploring how similar graphs are is an important primitive when comparing patterns in complex networks. There are a lot of different distance measures between graphs, and they are often based on comparing features that are derived from (algebraic representations of) the graph structures. Examples are distance measures based on spectral features, or computing some subgraph statistics such as graphlets or graph kernels. Comparing such graph features is powerful, but it often does not show where exactly one graph is different from the other one, or how the two graphs align.

Optimal transport (OT) based graph distances have become prominent recently and they address these challenges. Basically, OT-based graph distances associate a probability distribution with each graph. Then two graphs can be compared by finding a transport plan (a mapping) between the two probability distributions that has the minimal transport cost. The transport plan with the minimal cost can then be used as an alignment of the two graphs that is interpretable and robust, and it highlights the changes between the graphs that are relevant for the computed distance.

Most OT-based methods for measuring network similarity so far have been proposed for undirected graphs. But in many applications we want to compare directed graphs. Extending OT-based distances to directed graphs is not simple, because the cost function(s) usually used in OT need a symmetric distance metric, and this is typically derived from the distances between nodes in the graph. To solve this problem, we look at two node-to-node distances that were developed for directed graphs: the Generalized Effective Resistance (GRD) and the Markov chain hitting time (HTD). With these distance measures we can compute OT-based graph distances also for directed graphs. In particular, we explore using these metrics for both Wasserstein (Earth Mover) and Gromov-Wasserstein based OT distances for graphs.

- Application: cell-cell communication networks
  - evaluate relative utility for clustering them (single-cell sequencing data)
  - intrinsically directional, challenging test case: data dropouts (missing connections and entities), outliers, noise
- Contributions
  - (i) two OT formulations (Wasserstein, Gromov Wasserstein) for directed graphs, based on hitting time and GRD
  - (ii) evaluation on simulated directed stochastic block models + patient cell-cell communication networks
- Outline
  - Section 2 related work; Section 3 node-to-node distances and two OT distances; Section 4 numerical illustrations on synthetic and real world data; short discussion and future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Exploring how similar graphs are is an important primitive when comparing patterns in complex networks. There are a lot of different distance measures between graphs, and they are often based on comparing features that are derived from (algebraic representations of) the graph structures. Examples are distance measures based on spectral features, or computing some subgraph statistics such as graphlets or graph kernels. Comparing such graph features is powerful, but it often does not show where exactly one graph is different from the other one, or how the two graphs align.

Optimal transport (OT) based graph distances have become prominent recently and they address these challenges. Basically, OT-based graph distances associate a probability distribution with each graph. Then two graphs can be compared by finding a transport plan (a mapping) between the two probability distributions that has the minimal transport cost. The transport plan with the minimal cost can then be used as an alignment of the two graphs that is interpretable and robust, and it highlights the changes between the graphs that are relevant for the computed distance.

Most OT-based methods for measuring network similarity so far have been proposed for undirected graphs. But in many applications we want to compare directed graphs. Extending OT-based distances to directed graphs is not simple, because the cost function(s) usually used in OT need a symmetric distance metric, and this is typically derived from the distances between nodes in the graph. To solve this problem, we look at two node-to-node distances that were developed for directed graphs: the Generalized Effective Resistance (GRD) and the Markov chain hitting time (HTD). With these distance measures we can compute OT-based graph distances also for directed graphs. In particular, we explore using these metrics for both Wasserstein (Earth Mover) and Gromov-Wasserstein based OT distances for graphs.

After establishing our OT-based distances for directed graphs, we evaluate how useful they are relative to each other for clustering cell-cell communication networks, which come up in the study of single-cell sequencing data. These networks are directional by nature and they are a challenging test case, since technical artifacts like data dropouts (e.g., missing connections and entities), outliers and noise are often present in them.

Contributions (i) We present and evaluate two OT formulations (Wasserstein and Gromov Wasserstein) for comparing directed graphs, based on two node-to-node distances for directed graphs, the Markov chain hitting time and the Generalized Effective Resistance (ii) We evaluate the proposed approaches with simulated directed stochastic block models and on a case study of cell-cell communication networks of patients.

Outline The rest of the paper is structured like this. In Section 2 we briefly outline some related work. In Section 3 we discuss two node-to-node distance measures for directed graphs, which we use to formulate two optimal transport distances between directed graphs. In Section 4 we show the utility of the different formulations with some numerical illustrations of these distances for synthetic and real world data. We end with a short discussion that outlines future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Exploring the similarities between graphs is a crucial primitive for comparing patterns in complex networks. A large variety of distance measures between graphs exist, often based on comparing features derived from (algebraic representations of) the graph structures. Examples include distance measures based on spectral features, or the computation of certain subgraph statistics such as graphlets [1] or graph kernels [2]. While comparing such graph features is powerful, it often does not elucidate where precisely one graph differs from another, or how two graphs align.

Optimal transport (OT) based graph distances [3,4] have risen to prominence recently and address these challenges. In a nutshell, OT-based graph distances associate a certain probability distribution with each graph. Two graphs can then be compared by finding a transport plan (a mapping) between those two probability distributions with the minimal transport cost [5]. The transport plan with the minimal cost can then be used as an interpretable and robust alignment of the two graphs, highlighting the changes between the graphs that are relevant to the computed distance.

To date, most OT-based methods for measuring network similarities have been proposed for undirected graphs. In many applications, however, we are interested in comparing directed graphs. Extending OT-based distances to directed graphs is not simple, as the cost function(s) typically employed within OT require a symmetric distance metric, typically derived from the distances between nodes in the graph. To address this problem, we consider two node-to-node distances developed for directed graphs: the Generalized Effective Resistance (GRD) [6] and Markov chain hitting time (HTD) [7]. With these distance measures, we can compute OT-based graph distances even for directed graphs. Specifically, we explore the use of these metrics for both Wasserstein (Earth Mover) and Gromov-Wasserstein based OT distances for graphs [5].

Having established our OT-based distances for directed graphs, we evaluate their relative utility for clustering cell-cell communication networks, which arise in the study of single-cell sequencing data. These networks are intrinsically directional and provide a challenging test case, as technical artifacts such as data dropouts (e.g., missing connections and entities), outliers, and noise are often present in them [8].

Contributions (i) We present and evaluate two OT formulations (Wasserstein and Gromov Wasserstein) to compare directed graphs based on two node-to-node distances for directed graphs, namely the Markov chain hitting time [7] and the Generalized Effective Resistance [6] (ii) We evaluate the proposed approaches with simulated directed stochastic block models and on a case study of patient cell-cell communication networks.

Outline The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 briefly outlines some related work. In Section 3, we discuss two node-to-node distance measures for directed graphs, which we use to formulate two optimal transport distances between directed graphs. In Section 4 we illustrate the utility of these formulations with numerical illustrations of these distances for synthetic and real world data. We close with a short discussion outlining future work.
